name: Chemistry
topics: Atomic structure and particulate nature of matter

questions.q: What is the atomic number of an atom?
o: Number of electron shells in the atom
Number of neutrons in the nucleus
Sum of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
Number of protons in the nucleus
questions.e: The atomic number of an atom is defined as the number of protons found in its nucleus. It is this number that identifies the element and also tells the number of electrons in a neutral atom.
questions.p: Atomic number na di number of protons wey dey inside di nucleus of di atom. Na dis number dey tell us wetin di element be, and e dey match di number of electrons wen atom neutral.

questions.q: Which of these subatomic particles carries a negative charge and has a mass that is negligible compared to that of a proton?
questions.e: The electron carries a negative charge of -1 and its mass is about 1/1836 of the mass of a proton, so it is considered negligible. Protons and neutrons have almost equal masses, while an alpha particle is heavier, made of 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
questions.p: Electron get negative charge (-1) and e light well well, e no near proton mass at all. Proton and neutron dem get almost same mass, while alpha particle heavy pass electron sotey.

questions.q: Chlorine exists as two naturally occurring isotopes: chlorine-35 (making up 75% of all chlorine atoms) and chlorine-37 (making up 25%). What is the relative atomic mass of chlorine, correct to one decimal place?
questions.e: Relative atomic mass = (35 x 75 + 37 x 25) / 100 = (2625 + 925)/100 = 3550/100 = 35.5. This weighted average matches the known relative atomic mass of chlorine.
questions.p: To find relative atomic mass, multiply each isotope mass with im percentage, add dem, then divide by 100: (35x75 + 37x25)/100 = 3550/100 = 35.5. Na dat value be di correct answer.

questions.q: An atom has a mass number of 40. When it reacts, it loses two electrons to form a stable ion containing 18 electrons. How many neutrons are present in the atom?
questions.e: Since the ion has 18 electrons and a charge of 2+, the neutral atom must have 18 + 2 = 20 protons. Number of neutrons = mass number - protons = 40 - 20 = 20.
questions.p: Since di ion get 18 electrons and charge na 2+, di neutral atom get 18 + 2 = 20 protons. Neutron = mass number minus protons = 40 - 20 = 20.

questions.q: Calculate the number of atoms present in 0.5 mole of calcium metal. (Avogadro's number = 6.02 x 10²³ mol⁻¹)
questions.e: Number of atoms = number of moles x Avogadro's number = 0.5 x 6.02 x 10²³ = 3.01 x 10²³ atoms. The other options come from wrong multiplication or division errors.
questions.p: Number of atoms = moles x Avogadro number = 0.5 x 6.02 x 10²³ = 3.01 x 10²³ atoms. Di oda options na from wrong multiplication or division mistake.

questions.q: Which scientist modified the periodic law to state that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number rather than their atomic mass?
questions.e: Henry Moseley used X-ray studies to show that atomic number, not atomic mass, determines the periodic properties of elements. This corrected the earlier law proposed by Mendeleev.
questions.p: Moseley na im use X-ray work show say na atomic number dey control how elements dey arrange, no be atomic mass. E be like im correct wetin Mendeleev talk before.

questions.q: In the modern periodic table, elements that belong to the same group have the same number of what?
questions.e: Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell (valence electrons), which gives them similar chemical properties.
questions.p: Elements wey dey same group get same number of electron for dia outside shell (valence electrons), na why dem get similar chemical behaviour.

questions.q: Sodium (Na) has atomic number 11 and electronic configuration 2,8,1. Which of the following elements is in the same group as sodium?
questions.e: Potassium has configuration 2,8,8,1, ending in 1 valence electron just like sodium (2,8,1). Both are in Group IA (alkali metals). Mg, Ca and Al have 2 or 3 valence electrons, so they belong to different groups.
questions.p: Potassium get configuration 2,8,8,1, e still end with 1 valence electron like sodium (2,8,1). Na so both dey Group IA, dem be alkali metals. Mg, Ca and Al no match because dem get 2 or 3 valence electrons.

questions.q: Across a period from left to right in the periodic table, atomic radius generally shows which trend?
o: decreases due to increase in nuclear charge
increases due to increase in shielding effect
increases due to decrease in nuclear charge
questions.e: As you move across a period, protons increase while electrons are added to the same shell, so the nuclear charge pulls the electrons closer, making the atomic radius smaller.
questions.p: As you dey move across period, protons dey increase but electrons dey enter same shell, so the nucleus dey pull the electrons close, e make the atomic size smaller.

questions.q: An atom X has electronic configuration 2,8,6. How many valence electrons does atom X have?
questions.e: The valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell. For the configuration 2,8,6, the last number (6) represents the valence electrons.
questions.p: Valence electrons na electrons wey dey the last shell. For 2,8,6, the last number (6) na the valence electrons.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why ionisation energy generally decreases down a group, even though nuclear charge increases down the group?
o: decrease in number of principal energy levels down the group
increase in atomic radius and electron shielding down the group
increase in electron affinity down the group
decrease in number of protons down the group
questions.e: Down a group, extra electron shells are added, increasing atomic radius and the shielding effect from inner electrons. This weakens the pull of the nucleus on the outer electron, so less energy is needed to remove it, even though the nuclear charge is higher.
questions.p: As you go down group, extra electron shells dey add, so atomic size and shielding effect dey increase. This one weak the pull wey nucleus get for the outer electron, so small energy fit remove am, even though nuclear charge don increase.

questions.q: Which type of chemical bond is formed when one atom transfers electron(s) to another atom, producing oppositely charged ions that attract each other?
questions.e: An ionic bond is formed when a metal atom loses electrons to a non-metal atom, forming a cation and an anion. The oppositely charged ions then attract strongly, as seen in NaCl.
questions.p: Ionic bond na when metal atom comot electron give non-metal atom, so cation and anion go form. Dis two ion wey get opposite charge go attract each other strong, like for NaCl.

questions.q: Which of these compounds contains only covalent bonds between its atoms?
questions.e: CO₂ is made up of two non-metals, carbon and oxygen, which share electrons to form covalent bonds. NaCl, MgO and KBr are all formed between a metal and a non-metal, so they are ionic compounds.
questions.p: CO₂ na from two non-metal, carbon and oxygen, wey share electron make covalent bond. NaCl, MgO and KBr na metal join non-metal, so dem be ionic compound.

questions.q: In a chlorine molecule, Cl₂, each chlorine atom originally has 7 electrons in its outermost shell. When the two atoms combine by sharing one pair of electrons, how many electrons appear to surround each chlorine atom in the molecule, according to the octet rule?
questions.e: Each chlorine atom has 7 electrons of its own plus 1 shared electron from the other atom, giving it 8 electrons around it. This satisfies the octet rule, making the molecule stable.
questions.p: Each chlorine atom get im own 7 electron plus 1 wey dem share from the other atom, so e go reach 8 electron around am. Dis one follow the octet rule wey make the molecule stable.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical property of ionic compounds?
o: Good solubility in polar solvents like water
Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water
Low melting point and high volatility
questions.e: Ionic compounds have strong electrostatic forces between ions, which give them high melting points, not low ones. Low melting point and easy evaporation (volatility) are features of simple covalent/molecular compounds instead.
questions.p: Ionic compound get strong force wey hold di ions, so dem get high melting point, no be low one. Low melting point and quick evaporation na property of covalent compound.

questions.q: The electronegativity values of four elements are: Potassium (K) = 0.8, Hydrogen (H) = 2.1, Carbon (C) = 2.5, Oxygen (O) = 3.5. Based on these values, which pair of elements would form a bond with the greatest ionic character?
questions.e: The larger the electronegativity difference between two atoms, the more ionic the bond. K and O have the largest difference (3.5 - 0.8 = 2.7), which is greater than for the other pairs, so their bond is most ionic.
questions.p: Di bigger di difference for electronegativity, na so di bond go dey more ionic. K and O get di biggest difference (3.5 - 0.8 = 2.7) pass di oda pairs, so dia bond go dey most ionic.

questions.q: Diamond and graphite are both allotropes of carbon, yet graphite conducts electricity while diamond does not. Which statement best explains this difference in terms of bonding?
o: Graphite contains free-moving ions while diamond does not contain any ions
Diamond has metallic bonding while graphite has purely covalent bonding
Graphite has ionic bonds between its layers while diamond has only covalent bonds
In graphite, each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds leaving one delocalised electron free to move, while in diamond each carbon forms four covalent bonds with no free electrons
questions.e: In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to only three other carbon atoms, so one electron per atom is delocalised and free to move between layers, allowing it to conduct electricity. In diamond, each carbon forms four strong covalent bonds, using up all electrons so none are free to carry charge.
questions.p: For graphite, each carbon atom bond to only three oda carbon, so one electron go free waka within di layers, dat one make am conduct current. For diamond, each carbon bond strong to four oda carbon, so all di electrons dey used up, no free electron remain to carry current.

questions.q: Calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide, NaOH, present in 20 g of the compound. [Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1]
questions.e: Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g/mol. Number of moles = mass/molar mass = 20/40 = 0.5 mol.
questions.p: Molar mass of NaOH na 23+16+1 = 40 g/mol. Moles = mass over molar mass = 20/40 = 0.5 mol.

questions.q: What is the mass of 0.25 mole of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), CaCO₃? [Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16]
questions.e: Molar mass of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + (16x3) = 100 g/mol. Mass = moles x molar mass = 0.25 x 100 = 25 g.
questions.p: Molar mass of CaCO₃ na 40+12+(16x3) = 100 g/mol. Mass = moles x molar mass = 0.25 x 100 = 25 g.

questions.q: Calculate the number of molecules present in 4.4 g of carbon(IV) oxide, CO₂. [C = 12, O = 16, Avogadro's number = 6.02 x 10²³ mol⁻¹]
questions.e: Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + (16x2) = 44 g/mol. Moles = 4.4/44 = 0.1 mol. Number of molecules = 0.1 x 6.02x10²³ = 6.02x10²² molecules.
questions.p: Molar mass of CO₂ na 12+(16x2) = 44 g/mol. Moles = 4.4/44 = 0.1 mol. Number of molecules = 0.1 x 6.02x10²³ = 6.02x10²² molecules.

questions.q: What volume, at standard temperature and pressure (s.t.p), will be occupied by 0.2 mole of oxygen gas, O₂? [Molar volume of a gas at s.t.p = 22.4 dm3/mol]
questions.e: Volume = number of moles x molar volume = 0.2 x 22.4 dm3/mol = 4.48 dm3.
questions.p: Volume = number of moles x molar volume = 0.2 x 22.4 dm3/mol = 4.48 dm3.

questions.q: Magnesium reacts with excess hydrochloric acid according to the equation: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl₂ + H₂. If 3.0 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess acid, calculate the volume of hydrogen gas produced at s.t.p. [Mg = 24, Molar volume of a gas at s.t.p = 22.4 dm3/mol]
questions.e: Moles of Mg = 3.0/24 = 0.125 mol. From the equation, 1 mole Mg produces 1 mole H₂, so moles of H₂ = 0.125 mol. Volume of H₂ = 0.125 x 22.4 = 2.8 dm3.
questions.p: Moles of Mg = 3.0/24 = 0.125 mol. From the equation, 1 mole Mg go give 1 mole H₂, so moles of H₂ = 0.125 mol. Volume of H₂ = 0.125 x 22.4 = 2.8 dm3.

questions.q: A compound was found to contain, by mass, 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen. Determine the empirical formula of the compound. [C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]
questions.e: Divide each percentage by its atomic mass: C = 40/12 = 3.33, H = 6.7/1 = 6.7, O = 53.3/16 = 3.33. Dividing by the smallest value (3.33) gives C:H:O = 1:2:1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O.
questions.p: Divide each percentage by im atomic mass: C = 40/12 = 3.33, H = 6.7/1 = 6.7, O = 53.3/16 = 3.33. Divide everything by the smallest number (3.33) e go give C:H:O = 1:2:1, so empirical formula na CH₂O.

questions.q: A gas occupies 400 cm³ at a pressure of 2 atm. If the temperature is kept constant, what volume will the gas occupy when the pressure is increased to 4 atm?
questions.e: By Boyle's law, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ at constant temperature. So 2 x 400 = 4 x V₂, which gives V₂ = 800/4 = 200 cm³.
questions.p: Boyle law talk say P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ if temperature no change. So 2 x 400 = 4 x V₂, make V₂ = 800/4 = 200 cm³.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct basic assumption of the kinetic theory of gases?
o: All gas molecules possess the same kinetic energy at a given temperature regardless of mass
Gas molecules attract one another strongly
Gas molecules occupy a volume that is negligible compared to the volume of the container
Gas molecules move only in straight lines without ever colliding
questions.e: The kinetic theory assumes that gas molecules are so small that their actual volume is negligible compared to the volume of the container they occupy. The other options wrongly describe gas behaviour, since real gas molecules do collide and have varying energies.
questions.p: Kinetic theory dey assume say gas molecules dey very small, so their own volume no mean anything compared to the container volume. The other options no correct because molecules dey collide and their energy no equal for every molecule.

questions.q: A sample of gas has a volume of 300 cm³ at 27°C. At constant pressure, what will be its volume at 127°C?
questions.e: Convert to Kelvin: 27°C = 300 K, 127°C = 400 K. By Charles's law, V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂, so V₂ = 300 x 400/300 = 400 cm³.
questions.p: Convert to Kelvin: 27°C be 300 K, 127°C be 400 K. Charles law say V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂, so V₂ = 300 x 400/300 = 400 cm³.

questions.q: A fixed mass of gas in a closed container has a pressure of 1.5 atm at 300 K. If the volume is kept constant and the gas is heated to 600 K, what will its new pressure be?
questions.e: At constant volume, pressure law states P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂. So P₂ = 1.5 x 600/300 = 3.0 atm. Doubling the Kelvin temperature doubles the pressure when volume is fixed.
questions.p: When volume no change, pressure law talk say P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂. So P₂ = 1.5 x 600/300 = 3.0 atm. If you double the Kelvin temperature, pressure go double too.

questions.q: A gas occupies 250 cm³ at 27°C and 1 atm pressure. What will be its volume at standard temperature (0°C), the pressure remaining at 1 atm?
questions.e: Convert temperatures to Kelvin: 27°C = 300 K, 0°C = 273 K. By Charles's law, V₂ = V₁ x T₂/T₁ = 250 x 273/300 = 227.5 cm³. The volume reduces because the gas is cooled at constant pressure.
questions.p: Change the temperature to Kelvin: 27°C na 300 K, 0°C na 273 K. Charles law give V₂ = 250 x 273/300 = 227.5 cm³. The volume go reduce because dem cool the gas while pressure stay the same.

questions.q: Gas A has a molar mass of 16 g/mol and gas B has a molar mass of 64 g/mol. Using Graham's law of diffusion, what is the ratio of the rate of diffusion of gas A to that of gas B?
questions.e: Graham's law states rate A / rate B = √(M_B/M_A). So rate A/rate B = √(64/16) = √4 = 2. This means gas A diffuses twice as fast as gas B, giving a ratio of 2:1.
questions.p: Graham law talk say rate A / rate B = √(M_B/M_A). So rate A/rate B = √(64/16) = √4 = 2. Na im mean say gas A dey diffuse two times faster pass gas B, so ratio na 2:1.

questions.q: A solution that contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given quantity of solvent at a particular temperature, with undissolved solute still present at the bottom, is called a/an:
questions.e: A saturated solution holds the maximum solute possible at that temperature, so any extra solute stays undissolved at the bottom. This is different from a dilute or unsaturated solution, which can still dissolve more solute.
questions.p: Saturated solution na solution wey don carry the maximum solute wey e fit carry for that temperature, so any extra solute go remain for ground. E different from dilute or unsaturated solution wey still fit dissolve more solute.

questions.q: A village stream in Enugu State contains dissolved calcium hydrogencarbonate, causing temporary hardness. Which method will most effectively remove this type of hardness?
o: Adding common salt to the water
Dissolving more calcium hydrogencarbonate in it
questions.e: Boiling decomposes calcium hydrogencarbonate into insoluble calcium carbonate, carbon dioxide and water, removing the hardness. Filtering only removes solid particles, while adding salt or more hardness-causing substance does not remove hardness.
questions.p: If you boil the water, the calcium hydrogencarbonate go break down to calcium carbonate (wey no dey dissolve), CO₂ and water, so the hardness go comot. Filtering na only for solid particles, e no fit remove dissolved hardness.

questions.q: At 45°C, 25 g of sodium chloride dissolves completely in 50 g of water to form a saturated solution. What is the solubility of sodium chloride at this temperature, expressed in grams per 100 g of water?
questions.e: Solubility is usually expressed per 100 g of water. Since 25 g dissolves in 50 g of water, scaling up (multiply by 2) gives 50 g dissolving in 100 g of water, so the solubility is 50 g/100 g of water.
questions.p: Dem dey measure solubility per 100 g of water. Since 25 g dissolve for 50 g water, if you double am (times 2), e go be 50 g wey go dissolve for 100 g water. So solubility na 50 g/100 g water.

questions.q: The solubility of potassium trioxonitrate(V), KNO₃, in water at 60°C is 110 g per 100 g of water. What mass of KNO₃ is required to just saturate 250 g of water at this temperature?
questions.e: Solubility of 110 g per 100 g of water means for 250 g of water, you multiply 110 by (250/100) = 2.5. This gives 110 x 2.5 = 275 g of KNO₃ needed to saturate the water.
questions.p: Solubility na 110 g per 100 g water, so for 250 g water, you go multiply 110 by (250/100) wey be 2.5. 110 x 2.5 go give you 275 g KNO₃ wey go saturate the water.

questions.q: The solubility of a salt X is 90 g per 100 g of water at 90°C and 30 g per 100 g of water at 10°C. A saturated solution of X is prepared using 400 g of water at 90°C and then slowly cooled to 10°C without any loss of water by evaporation. Calculate the mass of crystals of X that will separate out on cooling.
questions.e: At 90°C, mass dissolved in 400 g water = (90/100) x 400 = 360 g. At 10°C, only (30/100) x 400 = 120 g can stay dissolved. The excess that crystallises out = 360 g - 120 g = 240 g.
questions.p: For 90°C, the mass wey dissolve for 400 g water na (90/100) x 400 = 360 g. For 10°C, na only (30/100) x 400 = 120 g fit still dissolve. So the extra wey go turn to crystal na 360 g - 120 g = 240 g.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes how the solubility of a gas such as carbon(IV) oxide in water is affected by changes in temperature and pressure?
o: It decreases with an increase in pressure
It increases with an increase in temperature
It is independent of temperature and pressure
It increases with an increase in pressure
questions.e: Gas solubility in a liquid increases as the pressure of the gas above the liquid increases, as stated by Henry's Law, and it decreases as temperature rises because the gas molecules gain energy and escape more easily. So the correct behaviour is that solubility increases with increased pressure.
questions.p: Gas dey more soluble for water as the pressure wey dey push the gas enter the liquid dey increase (na so Henry's Law talk am), but e dey less soluble as temperature dey rise because the gas molecules go get more energy make dem waka comot. So the correct one be say solubility dey increase as pressure dey increase.

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly defines an acid according to the Bronsted-Lowry theory?
o: A substance that donates a hydrogen ion (proton) to another substance
A substance that accepts a pair of electrons from another substance
A substance that releases hydroxide ions in aqueous solution
A substance that accepts a hydrogen ion from another substance
questions.e: A Bronsted-Lowry acid is defined as a proton (H+) donor. Option D describes a base, while B describes a Lewis acid and C describes an Arrhenius base.
questions.p: Bronsted-Lowry acid na substance wey dey give out proton (H+). Option D na base im be, B na Lewis acid, C na Arrhenius base definition.

questions.q: A sample of orange juice sold at Mile 12 market, Lagos, has a hydrogen ion concentration of 1 x 10⁻⁴ mol/dm3. What is the pH of the juice?
questions.e: pH = -log10[H+]. Since [H+] = 1 x 10⁻⁴, pH = -log10(1 x 10⁻⁴) = 4. This shows the juice is acidic, as expected for citrus fruit.
questions.p: pH = -log10[H+]. Since [H+] na 1 x 10⁻⁴, pH go be -log10(1 x 10⁻⁴) = 4. Na this one show say the juice dey acidic, as e suppose be for orange.

questions.q: Which of these salts would form an acidic solution when dissolved in water, given that it is produced from the reaction between a strong acid and a weak base?
questions.e: NH₄Cl is formed from hydrochloric acid (strong acid) and ammonia solution (weak base). The ammonium ion hydrolyses in water to release H+ ions, making the solution acidic.
questions.p: NH₄Cl na from hydrochloric acid (strong acid) and ammonia (weak base). The ammonium ion go hydrolyse for water release H+ ions, so e go make the solution acidic.

questions.q: Which indicator remains colourless in an acidic solution but turns pink when added to an alkaline solution?
questions.e: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic and neutral solutions but turns pink in alkaline (basic) solutions, making it a common indicator for titrations involving bases.
questions.p: Phenolphthalein no get colour for acidic and neutral solution, but e go turn pink for alkaline (basic) solution, na why dem dey use am well-well for titration wey involve base.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines oxidation in terms of electron transfer?
questions.e: Oxidation is the process in which an atom, ion or molecule loses electrons. This loss causes the oxidation number of the species to increase.
questions.p: Oxidation na when atom, ion or molecule lose electron. Wen electron comot, di oxidation number go increase.

questions.q: Determine the oxidation number of manganese in potassium tetraoxomanganate(VII), KMnO₄.
questions.e: Potassium is +1 and the four oxygens total -8 (4 x -2). For the neutral compound, +1 + Mn - 8 = 0, so Mn = +7.
questions.p: Potassium na +1, di four oxygen togeda na -8 (4 x -2). Since compound neutral, +1 + Mn - 8 = 0, so Mn = +7.

questions.q: In the reaction Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) -> ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s), which substance acts as the oxidizing agent?
questions.e: Zinc loses electrons and is oxidized, while the Cu₂+ ion in CuSO₄ gains those electrons and is reduced. The species that is reduced (accepts electrons) is the oxidizing agent, so CuSO₄ is the oxidizing agent.
questions.p: Zinc dey lose electron so im dey oxidize, while Cu₂+ for CuSO₄ dey collect di electron so im dey reduce. Di one wey dey collect electron na im be oxidizing agent, so na CuSO₄.

questions.q: In the ionic equation MnO₄⁻(aq) + 5Fe₂+(aq) + 8H+(aq) -> Mn₂+(aq) + 5Fe₃+(aq) + 4H₂O(l), how does the oxidation number of manganese change?
questions.e: Manganese starts as +7 in MnO₄⁻ and ends as +2 in Mn₂+. The change is 2 - 7 = -5, meaning the oxidation number decreases by 5, showing manganese is reduced.
questions.p: Manganese start as +7 for MnO₄⁻ and e end as +2 for Mn₂+. Di change na 2 - 7 = -5, meaning di oxidation number reduce by 5, so manganese don undergo reduction.

questions.q: Which of the following reactions is a redox (oxidation-reduction) reaction?
questions.e: In Zn + 2HCl, zinc changes from 0 to +2 (oxidized) while hydrogen changes from +1 to 0 (reduced), so electrons are transferred. The other three reactions are simple acid-base or double decomposition (precipitation) reactions with no change in oxidation numbers.
questions.p: For Zn + 2HCl, zinc change from 0 to +2 (oxidation) while hydrogen change from +1 to 0 (reduction), so electron transfer dey happen. Di oda three na just acid-base or double decomposition wey no get change for oxidation number.

questions.q: During electrolysis, at which electrode does reduction (gain of electrons) take place?
questions.e: The cathode is connected to the negative terminal of the battery, so positive ions (cations) move there and gain electrons, which is reduction. Oxidation (loss of electrons) happens at the anode instead.
questions.p: Cathode na where reduction dey happen because positive ions (cations) dey go there collect electron. Na opposite thing dey happen for anode, wey be oxidation.

questions.q: Molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr₂, is electrolysed using inert graphite electrodes. What product is formed at the cathode?
questions.e: In molten PbBr₂ there are only Pb₂+ and Br- ions present (no water). Pb₂+ ions move to the cathode and gain electrons to form lead metal, while Br- ions move to the anode and are oxidised to bromine gas.
questions.p: Since na only Pb₂+ and Br- ions dey inside the melt (no water), the Pb₂+ go go cathode take electron turn to lead metal. Na the Br- dey go anode become bromine gas.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of dilute aqueous sodium chloride using inert electrodes, which ion is discharged at the cathode instead of the sodium ion?
questions.e: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so Na+ stays in solution while H+ (from water) is preferentially discharged at the cathode to form hydrogen gas. This follows the rule of selective (preferential) discharge based on position in the electrochemical series.
questions.p: Sodium reactive pass hydrogen, so Na+ no dey discharge; na the H+ wey come from water dey discharge for cathode produce hydrogen gas. Na the rule of selective discharge dey explain am.

questions.q: A steady current of 5 amperes is passed through a solution of copper(II) sulphate for 3860 seconds using inert electrodes. Calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode. [1 Faraday = 96500 C/mol, Cu = 64, Cu₂+ requires 2 electrons per atom deposited]
questions.e: Charge, Q = I x t = 5 x 3860 = 19300 C. Moles of electrons = 19300/96500 = 0.2 mol. Since Cu₂+ + 2e- gives Cu, moles of Cu = 0.2/2 = 0.1 mol, so mass = 0.1 x 64 = 6.4 g.
questions.p: Charge Q = I x t = 5 x 3860 = 19300 C. Moles of electron = 19300/96500 = 0.2 mol. Since na 2 electrons per Cu₂+, moles of Cu = 0.1 mol, mass = 0.1 x 64 = 6.4 g.

questions.q: Two electrolytic cells are connected in series: the first contains silver nitrate solution and the second contains copper(II) sulphate solution. If the same quantity of electricity deposits 0.54 g of silver in the first cell, what mass of copper is deposited in the second cell? [Ag = 108, Cu = 64; Ag+ + e- -> Ag; Cu₂+ + 2e- -> Cu]
questions.e: Moles of Ag deposited = 0.54/108 = 0.005 mol, and since 1 electron deposits 1 Ag atom, moles of electrons passed = 0.005 mol. The same charge passes through the series circuit, so moles of Cu = 0.005/2 = 0.0025 mol (because Cu needs 2 electrons per atom), giving mass = 0.0025 x 64 = 0.16 g.
questions.p: Moles of Ag wey deposit = 0.54/108 = 0.005 mol, and na 1 electron dey deposit 1 Ag atom, so moles of electron wey pass = 0.005 mol. Na the same charge dey pass for the two cells wey dey series, so moles of Cu = 0.005/2 = 0.0025 mol, mass = 0.0025 x 64 = 0.16 g.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes an exothermic reaction?
o: a reaction that only occurs at very high temperature
a reaction that requires continuous heating to proceed
a reaction that releases heat to the surroundings
a reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings
questions.e: An exothermic reaction gives out heat energy to the surroundings, so the surroundings get warmer. This is the standard definition used in WAEC chemistry.
questions.p: Exothermic reaction na reaction wey dey release heat go the surrounding, so the environment go hot small. Na so WAEC chemistry dey define am.

questions.q: Which of the following processes is endothermic?
o: neutralization of sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid
combustion of methane gas in air
rusting of an iron nail exposed to air and moisture
questions.e: When ammonium nitrate dissolves in water, it absorbs heat from the water, making the solution feel cold. Combustion, neutralization and rusting all release heat, so they are exothermic.
questions.p: When ammonium nitrate dissolve for water, e dey absorb heat from the water make solution cold. Combustion, neutralization and rusting dey release heat, so dem be exothermic.

questions.q: A student dissolves a sample of sodium hydroxide pellets in 100 cm³ of water in a plastic cup calorimeter. The temperature of the water rises from 25°C to 33°C. Given that the specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 J/g°C and the density of water is 1 g/cm³, calculate the quantity of heat released during the dissolution.
questions.e: Mass of water = 100 g (density 1 g/cm3). Temperature change = 33 - 25 = 8°C. Heat = mc(delta T) = 100 x 4.2 x 8 = 3360 J.
questions.p: Mass of water na 100 g because density na 1 g/cm3. Temperature change na 33 minus 25 wey be 8°C. Heat = mc(delta T) = 100 x 4.2 x 8 = 3360 J.

questions.q: Using the bond energies H-H = 436 kJ/mol, Cl-Cl = 242 kJ/mol and H-Cl = 431 kJ/mol, calculate the enthalpy change, delta H, for the reaction: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) -> 2HCl(g)
questions.e: Delta H = (bonds broken) - (bonds formed) = (436 + 242) - (2 x 431) = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol. The negative sign shows the reaction releases energy, so it is exothermic.
questions.p: Delta H = (bonds wey break) - (bonds wey form) = (436 + 242) - (2 x 431) = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol. The minus sign show say the reaction dey release energy, so na exothermic.

questions.q: In the energy level diagram for a certain reaction, the reactants are at an energy level of 50 kJ, the products are at 20 kJ, and the peak of the curve representing the activated complex is at 90 kJ. What is the activation energy of the forward reaction, and is the overall reaction exothermic or endothermic?
o: Activation energy = 30 kJ; the reaction is exothermic
Activation energy = 40 kJ; the reaction is exothermic
Activation energy = 40 kJ; the reaction is endothermic
Activation energy = 70 kJ; the reaction is endothermic
questions.e: Activation energy is the difference between the peak and the reactants: 90 - 50 = 40 kJ. Since products (20 kJ) are lower in energy than reactants (50 kJ), the reaction releases energy overall, making it exothermic.
questions.p: Activation energy na the gap between the peak and reactants: 90 - 50 = 40 kJ. Since products (20 kJ) dey lower pass reactants (50 kJ), the reaction dey release energy overall, so na exothermic.

questions.q: A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction mainly by
o: increasing the concentration of the reactants
increasing the activation energy required for the reaction
increasing the temperature of the reacting substances
providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
questions.e: A catalyst works by offering a different route for the reaction that needs less activation energy, so more molecules can react successfully. It does not change the temperature or concentration of reactants.
questions.p: Catalyst dey work by giving another road for the reaction wey need less activation energy, so plenty molecules fit react well well. E no dey change temperature or concentration of the reactants.

questions.q: A catalyst is best described as a substance that
o: speeds up a reaction without itself being used up permanently
increases the mass of the products formed
changes the identity of the products formed
slows down a reaction and remains unchanged
questions.e: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction path with lower activation energy, so it speeds up the reaction but it is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.
questions.p: Catalyst na substance wey dey make reaction fast pass, but e no dey finish or change for the process; e remain the same after the reaction.

questions.q: During an experiment, zinc granules reacted with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. A pupil collected 48 cm³ of hydrogen gas after 12 seconds. Calculate the average rate of the reaction in cm³ per second.
questions.e: Rate = volume of gas produced / time taken = 48 cm³ / 12 s = 4 cm³/s.
questions.p: Rate = volume wey dem collect divide by time = 48 cm³ / 12 s = 4 cm³/s.

questions.q: A student compared the reaction of dilute hydrochloric acid with (i) a lump of calcium carbonate and (ii) powdered calcium carbonate of the same mass. The powdered form reacted much faster. What is the best explanation for this observation?
o: The powdered form is more concentrated than the lump
The powdered form has a larger surface area exposed to the acid, allowing more collisions per second
The powdered form has a lower activation energy than the lump
The powdered form has fewer particles than the lump
questions.e: Powdering the solid increases the total surface area in contact with the acid, so acid particles can collide with carbonate particles more often, increasing the rate of reaction.
questions.p: When dem grind the solid to powder, e get bigger surface area wey the acid go touch, so collision dey happen pass, dat na why rate increase.

questions.q: The rate of a particular reaction is found to double for every 10°C rise in temperature. If the rate of the reaction at 20°C is 2.0 mol/dm³/s, what will be the rate at 50°C?
questions.e: The temperature rises by 50-20 = 30°C, which is 3 steps of 10°C. The rate doubles 3 times, so new rate = 2.0 x 2³ = 2.0 x 8 = 16.0 mol/dm³/s.
questions.p: Temperature increase na 50-20 = 30°C, wey be 3 times of 10°C. Since rate dey double for each 10°C, e go double 3 times: 2.0 x 2³ = 16.0 mol/dm³/s.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a chemical system that has reached equilibrium?
o: The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate so concentrations stay constant
All the reactants have been converted to products
The concentrations of reactants and products are exactly equal
The reaction has completely stopped and no particles are moving
questions.e: At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions still occur but at equal rates, so the amounts of reactants and products no longer change. The reaction does not stop; it is dynamic, not static.
questions.p: For equilibrium, both forward and backward reaction dey still happen, but dem dey happen for same speed, so the amount of reactant and product no dey change again. E no mean say reaction don stop.

questions.q: Consider the reversible reaction: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) <=> 2NH₃(g), ΔH = -92 kJ/mol (the Haber process). Which change would increase the yield of ammonia at equilibrium, according to Le Chatelier's principle?
o: Continuously removing nitrogen gas from the system
Raising the temperature of the system
Increasing the pressure on the system
Lowering the pressure on the system
questions.e: There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles on the right, so increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles, which is the ammonia side. This increases the yield of NH₃.
questions.p: For the left side, mole of gas na 4, for right side na 2. If you increase pressure, equilibrium go shift go the side wey get small mole, wey be ammonia side. So ammonia go increase.

questions.q: For the equilibrium reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) <=> 2SO₃(g), ΔH = -198 kJ/mol, what happens to the equilibrium position when the temperature of the system is increased?
o: It shifts to the left, decreasing the yield of SO₃
The equilibrium constant, Kc, increases while the position stays the same
It shifts to the right, increasing the yield of SO₃
It remains unchanged because temperature does not affect equilibrium
questions.e: The forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH is negative), so increasing temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction to absorb the extra heat. This shifts the equilibrium to the left, reducing SO₃ yield.
questions.p: The forward reaction na exothermic one (ΔH negative), so if you increase heat, the system go favour the backward reaction wey dey absorb heat. Equilibrium go shift go left, and SO₃ go reduce.

questions.q: A chemist, Mrs Adeyemi, set up the equilibrium H₂(g) + I₂(g) <=> 2HI(g) in a 2 dm³ sealed flask. At equilibrium, the flask contained 0.4 mol of H₂, 0.4 mol of I₂ and 0.8 mol of HI. What is the value of the equilibrium constant, Kc, for this reaction?
questions.e: Divide each mole value by the volume (2 dm³) to get concentrations: [H₂]=0.2, [I₂]=0.2, [HI]=0.4 mol/dm³. Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]) = (0.4)² / (0.2 x 0.2) = 0.16/0.04 = 4.
questions.p: First divide each mole by the volume (2 dm³): [H₂]=0.2, [I₂]=0.2, [HI]=0.4. Then Kc = (0.4)² divide by (0.2 x 0.2) = 0.16/0.04 = 4.

questions.q: 2.0 mol of PCl₅(g) was placed in a 1 dm³ sealed container and allowed to reach equilibrium according to PCl₅(g) <=> PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g). At equilibrium, 0.5 mol of Cl₂ gas was present. Calculate the equilibrium constant, Kc, for this reaction.
questions.e: Since 0.5 mol of Cl₂ formed, 0.5 mol of PCl₃ also formed and 0.5 mol of PCl₅ was used up. Equilibrium amounts (in a 1 dm³ flask, so moles = concentration) are PCl₅ = 1.5, PCl₃ = 0.5, Cl₂ = 0.5. Kc = (0.5 x 0.5) / 1.5 = 0.25/1.5 = 0.167.
questions.p: Since 0.5 mol Cl₂ form, 0.5 mol PCl₃ too form, and 0.5 mol PCl₅ don use up. So at equilibrium: PCl₅ = 1.5, PCl₃ = 0.5, Cl₂ = 0.5 (volume na 1 dm³ so mole = concentration). Kc = (0.5 x 0.5)/1.5 = 0.167.

questions.q: What is the correct effect of adding a catalyst to a reversible reaction that has reached equilibrium?
o: It shifts the position of equilibrium towards the products
It speeds up the attainment of equilibrium without changing the value of Kc
It lowers the activation energy of the forward reaction only, not the reverse
It increases the yield of the products at equilibrium
questions.e: A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster, but the position of equilibrium and the value of Kc remain unchanged. It does not increase product yield.
questions.p: Catalyst dey speed up both forward and backward reaction for the same way, so equilibrium go reach fast, but the position of equilibrium and Kc no go change. E no dey increase product yield.

questions.q: In a school laboratory, a technician wants to prepare hydrogen gas quickly using a metal and dilute hydrochloric acid. Which of these metals is most suitable for this preparation?
questions.e: Zinc is reactive enough to displace hydrogen from dilute acids, unlike copper, silver and mercury which are below hydrogen in the reactivity series and do not react with dilute HCl.
questions.p: Zinc dey reactive well-well pass hydrogen for di reactivity series, so e fit push hydrogen comot from dilute acid. Copper, silver and mercury no reactive reach dat level.

questions.q: Chidinma bubbled a colourless gas into a test tube that contained a glowing wood splint, and the splint immediately burst into flame. Which gas did she most likely use?
questions.e: Oxygen supports combustion strongly, so it relights a glowing splint into a flame. Hydrogen pops with a flame already burning, carbon(IV) oxide and nitrogen both put out a glowing splint.
questions.p: Oxygen dey support fire well, na im dey make glowing splint burst into flame. Hydrogen dey pop wen flame dey burn already, but CO₂ and nitrogen go kill di glowing splint.

questions.q: Chlorine gas is commonly used industrially to bleach wood pulp and cotton fabrics. What is the main reason chlorine is able to remove colour from these materials?
o: It reduces the coloured substance by adding electrons to it
It neutralises the coloured dye through an acid-base reaction
It reacts with water to form an acid that oxidises the coloured substance to a colourless one
It simply dissolves the dye without any chemical change
questions.e: Chlorine reacts with water to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous (chloric(I)) acid; the hypochlorous acid is a strong oxidising agent that destroys the coloured compound, turning it colourless. This is an oxidation process, not reduction or neutralisation.
questions.p: Chlorine dey react with water make HCl and hypochlorous acid; di hypochlorous acid na strong oxidising agent wey dey destroy di colour, e turn am to colourless. Na oxidation, no be reduction or neutralisation.

questions.q: 25 cm3 of ammonia gas was completely burnt in excess oxygen according to the equation: 4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) -> 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g). If all volumes were measured at the same temperature and pressure, what volume of oxygen was used up?
questions.e: From the equation, 4 volumes of NH₃ react with 5 volumes of O₂. So volume of O₂ = (5/4) x 25 cm3 = 31.25 cm3. Gas volumes react in the same ratio as their mole ratio at constant temperature and pressure.
questions.p: From di equation, 4 volume NH₃ dey react with 5 volume O₂. So O₂ wey dem use = (5/4) x 25 cm3 = 31.25 cm3. Na because gas volumes dey react for di same ratio as dia mole ratio wen temperature and pressure no change.

questions.q: A colourless solution was tested as follows: a few drops of dilute nitric acid were added, followed by silver nitrate solution. A white precipitate formed, and this precipitate dissolved completely when dilute ammonia solution was added in excess. Which anion is most likely present in the original solution?
questions.e: Silver chloride forms a white precipitate that is soluble in dilute ammonia, while silver bromide (cream) and silver iodide (pale yellow) need concentrated ammonia or do not dissolve at all. Sulphate ions do not give a precipitate with silver nitrate under these acidic conditions.
questions.p: Silver chloride na white precipitate wey go dissolve for dilute ammonia, but silver bromide (cream) and silver iodide (pale yellow) need concentrated ammonia or no go dissolve at all. Sulphate no dey form precipitate with silver nitrate for dis kain acidic condition.

questions.q: Which of the following is a general physical property of metals?
o: They have very low melting points generally
They are brittle when hammered into sheets
They are good conductors of heat and electricity
They are poor conductors of electricity
questions.e: Metals have free-moving electrons (a 'sea of electrons') that allow them to conduct heat and electricity well. Most metals are also malleable (not brittle) and many have high melting points.
questions.p: Metal get electrons wey dey waka free inside am, na im dey make dem conduct heat and electricity well well. Most metals no dey brittle, dem dey bend well, and plenty of dem get high melting point.

questions.q: Aluminium is extracted industrially by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (in cryolite) rather than by reduction with carbon. The best reason for this is that:
o: Aluminium ore does not contain oxygen
Aluminium has a very low melting point
Carbon is more expensive than electricity in industry
Aluminium is too reactive for carbon to reduce its ore
questions.e: In the reactivity series, aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove oxygen from aluminium oxide. Only a stronger method like electrolysis can break the strong bond and free the aluminium metal.
questions.p: For reactivity series, aluminium pass carbon for strength, so carbon no fit remove oxygen from aluminium oxide. Na only electrolysis get power to break the strong bond free the aluminium.

questions.q: Rusting of an iron nail, like one left outside a Lagos workshop, occurs fastest when the nail is exposed to:
questions.e: Rusting is the reaction of iron with both oxygen and water (moisture) at the same time to form hydrated iron(III) oxide. Without either water or oxygen present together, rusting is very slow or does not occur.
questions.p: Rust dey happen when iron meet oxygen and water together, dem go form hydrated iron(III) oxide. If water or oxygen no dey, rust no go fast reach like that.

questions.q: Brass, a yellowish alloy often used for door handles and musical instruments, is made by combining:
questions.e: Brass is an alloy formed by mixing copper with zinc, which gives it a golden colour and makes it harder and more resistant to corrosion than pure copper. Bronze, not brass, is made from copper and tin.
questions.p: Brass na alloy wey dem mix copper with zinc together, e dey give am gold colour and e dey strong pass pure copper, e no too dey rust. Na bronze be copper and tin mixture, no be brass.

questions.q: A sample of zinc oxide weighing 8.10 g is completely reduced by carbon to produce zinc metal. Calculate the mass of zinc produced. [Zn = 65, O = 16]
questions.e: Molar mass of ZnO = 65 + 16 = 81 g/mol, so moles of ZnO = 8.10/81 = 0.1 mol. Since ZnO gives 1 mole of Zn per mole of ZnO, mass of Zn = 0.1 x 65 = 6.5 g.
questions.p: Molar mass of ZnO na 65 + 16 = 81 g/mol, so moles of ZnO na 8.10/81 = 0.1 mol. Since one ZnO dey give one Zn, mass of Zn na 0.1 x 65 = 6.5 g.

questions.q: Which metallic oxide below is amphoteric, meaning it can react with both acids and bases?
questions.e: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric because it reacts with acids like HCl to form aluminium salts and also reacts with bases like NaOH to form aluminates. Na₂O, MgO and CuO are basic oxides that react only with acids.
questions.p: Aluminium oxide na amphoteric oxide because e dey react with acid like HCl to form aluminium salt, e sef dey react with base like NaOH to form aluminate. Na₂O, MgO and CuO na basic oxide wey dey only react with acid.

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct general molecular formula for the homologous series of alkanes?
questions.e: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons containing only single carbon-carbon bonds. Their general formula is CnH2n+2, for example methane (CH₄, n=1) and ethane (C₂H₆, n=2).
questions.p: Alkane na saturated hydrocarbon wey get only single bond between di carbon atoms. Dat na why dia general formula na CnH2n+2, like methane CH₄ and ethane C₂H₆.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of the hydrocarbon with structural formula CH₃-CH₂-CH=CH₂?
questions.e: The compound has 4 carbon atoms with a double bond starting at the first carbon from the end, so it is named but-1-ene. The 'but' shows 4 carbons and '1-ene' shows the double bond position.
questions.p: Di compound get 4 carbon atoms and di double bond start from di first carbon, so dem go call am but-1-ene. 'But' mean 4 carbons, '1-ene' show say di double bond dey for position one.

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes alkenes from alkanes?
o: Alkenes decolourise bromine water rapidly while alkanes do not react with it under the same conditions
Alkenes are saturated hydrocarbons while alkanes are unsaturated
Alkanes burn with a more luminous and sooty flame than alkenes
Alkanes undergo addition reactions readily while alkenes undergo substitution reactions
questions.e: Alkenes contain a C=C double bond that is easily broken by addition reactions, so they quickly decolourise bromine water (orange to colourless). Alkanes, being saturated, do not react with bromine water under the same mild conditions.
questions.p: Alkene get C=C double bond wey dey easy to break through addition reaction, so e go quick turn bromine water from orange to no colour. Alkane na saturated hydrocarbon, e no go react with bromine water under dat same condition.

questions.q: Which property of benzene explains why it does not readily undergo addition reactions like typical alkenes, despite its ring appearing to have three double bonds?
o: Benzene has a high boiling point
Benzene contains only single bonds between its carbon atoms
Benzene's delocalized π electrons give it extra (aromatic) stability
questions.e: The six π electrons in benzene are delocalized evenly around the ring, making it unusually stable. This stability makes benzene resistant to addition reactions and favours substitution reactions instead.
questions.p: Di six π electrons for benzene dey spread evenly round di ring, dis one dey make am stable well-well. Because of dis stability, benzene no dey easily do addition reaction, e dey prefer substitution reaction instead.

questions.q: An alkene with general formula CnH2n was found to contain 85.7% carbon by mass and has a molar mass of 42 g/mol. What is the value of n? [C = 12, H = 1]
questions.e: Molar mass of CnH2n is 14n, so 14n = 42 gives n = 3. Checking: %C = (12x3)/(14x3) x100 = 85.7%, which matches the given data, confirming n = 3 (propene, C₃H₆).
questions.p: Molar mass of CnH2n na 14n, so 14n = 42 mean n = 3. If you check am, %C = (12x3)/(14x3) x100 = 85.7%, e match wetin dem give, so n = 3 (propene, C₃H₆).

questions.q: Propane burns completely in excess oxygen according to the equation: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ -> 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. What mass of carbon(IV) oxide is produced when 0.5 mole of propane burns completely? [C = 12, O = 16]
questions.e: From the equation, 1 mole of propane produces 3 moles of CO₂, so 0.5 mole produces 1.5 moles of CO₂. Mass of CO₂ = 1.5 x 44 = 66g.
questions.p: From di equation, 1 mole propane dey produce 3 mole CO₂, so 0.5 mole go produce 1.5 mole CO₂. Mass of CO₂ = 1.5 x 44 = 66g.

questions.q: Which of the following functional groups is present in all alcohols (alkanols)?
questions.e: Alcohols are organic compounds whose molecules contain the hydroxyl group, -OH, attached to a carbon chain. The other groups belong to acids, aldehydes and esters respectively, not alcohols.
questions.p: Alcohol na compound wey get -OH group for im molecule. The other groups na for acid, aldehyde and ester, no be alcohol.

questions.q: To which homologous series does ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, belong?
questions.e: Ethanoic acid contains the carboxyl group -COOH, which is the functional group that defines the alkanoic acid (carboxylic acid) homologous series. Alkanols have -OH and alkyl alkanoates (esters) have -COO-.
questions.p: Ethanoic acid get -COOH group, na im be the mark for alkanoic acid family. Alkanol get -OH while ester (alkyl alkanoate) get -COO-.

questions.q: When ethanol reacts with ethanoic acid in the presence of a few drops of concentrated trioxosulphate(VI) acid as catalyst, the products formed are:
questions.e: This is esterification: an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid, with conc. H₂SO₄ as catalyst and dehydrating agent, to form an ester and water. Ethanol + ethanoic acid gives ethyl ethanoate (the ester) and water.
questions.p: Dis na esterification: alcohol plus acid, wit conc. H₂SO₄ as catalyst, dey form ester and water. So ethanol plus ethanoic acid go give ethyl ethanoate and water.

questions.q: Which of the following compounds is an ester?
questions.e: Esters have the general functional group -COO- joining two carbon chains, as seen in CH₃COOCH₃ (methyl ethanoate). The other compounds are a carboxylic acid, an alcohol and an aldehyde respectively.
questions.p: Ester get -COO- group wey dey join two carbon chain, like for CH₃COOCH₃ (methyl ethanoate). The other ones na acid, alcohol and aldehyde.

questions.q: Which of the following polymers is produced by condensation polymerisation, with a small molecule such as water lost during the reaction?
questions.e: Nylon is made by condensation polymerisation of a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid, with water eliminated as each bond forms. Polyethene, PVC and polystyrene are all addition polymers formed from alkene-type monomers with no by-product lost.
questions.p: Nylon dey form from condensation polymerisation, wia diamine and diacid dey join and water dey comot. Polyethene, PVC and polystyrene na addition polymer, no by-product dey comot.

questions.q: A student prepares an ester by reacting methanoic acid with methanol. The product is methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃. What is the molar mass of this ester? [H=1, C=12, O=16]
questions.e: Methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃, has the formula C₂H₄O₂. Molar mass = (2 x 12) + (4 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 24 + 4 + 32 = 60 g/mol.
questions.p: Methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃, na C₂H₄O₂. Molar mass = (2 x 12) + (4 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 24 + 4 + 32 = 60 g/mol.

questions.q: Common salt dissolves completely in water to form a clear solution. Which separation technique will a chemist use to recover pure water from this salt solution?
questions.e: Salt does not evaporate with water, so when the solution is heated, the water vapour can be collected and condensed as pure water, leaving the salt behind. This process is called simple distillation.
questions.p: Salt no dey evaporate with water, so if you heat the solution, water go turn vapour wey you fit condense collect as pure water, salt go remain. Na simple distillation be dat.

questions.q: A laboratory technician in Kano has a mixture of iron filings and sulphur powder that must be separated without using any liquid or heat. Which method is most suitable?
o: Heat the mixture until it melts
Use a magnet to attract the iron filings
Filter the mixture through filter paper
questions.e: Iron is magnetic while sulphur is not, so a magnet can pull out the iron filings and leave the sulphur powder behind. This is a quick, dry method that needs no heat or liquid.
questions.p: Iron get magnetic property but sulphur no get am, so magnet go fish out the iron filings leave the sulphur. Na dry method wey no need heat or liquid.

questions.q: Pure benzoic acid melts sharply at 122°C. A student tests a sample of benzoic acid bought from a market in Onitsha and finds that it melts gradually between 114°C and 118°C. What does this show about the sample?
o: The sample is impure because it melts over a range and below the true melting point
Melting point cannot be used to test purity in this case
The sample is purer than the standard benzoic acid
The sample has the same purity as pure benzoic acid
questions.e: A pure substance melts sharply at a fixed, known temperature. Since this sample melts over a range and at a lower temperature than the known value for pure benzoic acid, it means impurities are present, which both lower and widen the melting point range.
questions.p: Pure substance dey melt sharp sharp for one fixed temperature. Since dis sample melt small small for range wey dey lower pass the correct value, e mean say impurity dey inside, wey dey reduce and widen the melting range.

questions.q: In a paper chromatography experiment carried out by a student to separate the dyes in a sample of ink, the solvent front travelled 9.0 cm from the starting line, while a particular dye spot travelled 3.6 cm from the same starting line. What is the Rf value of this dye?
questions.e: Rf value is calculated as distance moved by the solute divided by distance moved by the solvent. Rf = 3.6 cm / 9.0 cm = 0.4. This value has no unit because it is a ratio.
questions.p: Rf value na distance wey the solute waka divide by distance wey solvent waka. Rf = 3.6 cm / 9.0 cm = 0.4. E no get unit because na ratio.

questions.q: A mixture of ethanol (boiling point 78°C) and water (boiling point 100°C) is heated slowly using a fractionating column set up correctly for fractional distillation. Which statement correctly describes what happens as the mixture is heated?
o: Water vapour rises first and is collected before the ethanol vapour
Both liquids boil off together as one vapour with no separation
Ethanol vapour rises first through the column and is collected first because it has the lower boiling point
The fractionating column has no effect on the order of separation
questions.e: In fractional distillation, the liquid with the lower boiling point vaporises first and rises through the fractionating column to be collected first. Since ethanol boils at 78°C, which is lower than water's 100°C, ethanol vapour comes over first, while the column helps improve the separation by allowing repeated condensation and vaporisation.
questions.p: For fractional distillation, the liquid wey get lower boiling point go turn vapour first pass through the column come dey collected first. Ethanol dey boil for 78°C wey dey lower pass water own 100°C, so ethanol go comot first, the column dey help make the separation sharp well well.

questions.q: A student performed paper chromatography on an unknown food dye and found that the dye spot moved 4.5 cm while the solvent front moved 6.0 cm from the baseline. A reference chart gives the following standard Rf values: Dye A = 0.75, Dye B = 0.60, Dye C = 0.45, Dye D = 0.30. Which dye is most likely present in the unknown sample?
questions.e: First calculate the Rf value of the unknown spot: Rf = 4.5 cm / 6.0 cm = 0.75. Comparing this with the reference chart, 0.75 matches Dye A, so Dye A is most likely present.
questions.p: First calculate the Rf value: Rf = 4.5 cm / 6.0 cm = 0.75. If you compare am with the chart, 0.75 match Dye A, so na Dye A dey the sample.

questions.q: In the industrial manufacture of ammonia by the Haber process, which substance is used as the catalyst to speed up the reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen?
questions.e: The Haber process combines nitrogen and hydrogen to form ammonia, and finely divided iron is the standard catalyst used to speed up this reaction without being consumed.
questions.p: Haber process na im dem dey use make ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, and dem dey use finely divided iron as catalyst to speed up the reaction.

questions.q: Which acid is manufactured industrially using the Contact process, in which sulphur(IV) oxide is catalytically oxidised to sulphur(VI) oxide using vanadium(V) oxide?
questions.e: The Contact process converts sulphur(IV) oxide to sulphur(VI) oxide using vanadium(V) oxide as catalyst, and the sulphur(VI) oxide is then dissolved to produce sulphuric(VI) acid.
questions.p: Contact process na im dem dey convert sulphur(IV) oxide to sulphur(VI) oxide with vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, then dem use am make sulphuric(VI) acid.

questions.q: Factories in Kaduna that burn coal and diesel containing sulphur impurities release a gas into the air. When this gas dissolves in rain water, it forms acid rain that damages buildings and crops. Which gas is mainly responsible?
questions.e: Burning fossil fuels with sulphur impurities releases sulphur(IV) oxide, which dissolves in rain water to form a dilute acid, giving acid rain.
questions.p: When fossil fuel wey get sulphur dey burn, e dey release sulphur(IV) oxide, and dis gas go mix with rain water make am turn acid rain.

questions.q: A bag of fertilizer contains ammonium trioxonitrate(V), NH₄NO₃. Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in the compound. (N = 14, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.e: Molar mass of NH₄NO₃ = 14+4+14+48 = 80. There are 2 nitrogen atoms, mass = 28. Percentage N = (28/80) x 100 = 35.0%.
questions.p: Molar mass of NH₄NO₃ na 80, and nitrogen wey dey inside na 28 (2 N atoms). So percentage na (28/80) x 100 = 35.0%.

questions.q: A cement factory heats 500 kg of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), CaCO₃, strongly to decompose it into calcium oxide and carbon(IV) oxide. Calculate the mass of calcium oxide produced. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: CaCO₃ (molar mass 100) decomposes to give CaO (molar mass 56) in a 1:1 mole ratio. Mass of CaO = (56/100) x 500 kg = 280 kg.
questions.p: CaCO₃ get molar mass 100 and e dey break down to CaO (molar mass 56) one-to-one. So mass of CaO = (56/100) x 500 kg = 280 kg.

questions.q: Farmers along a river in Benue State apply excess nitrogenous fertilizer to their farms. Rain washes some of it into the river. What is the most likely effect of this on the aquatic life in the river?
o: Decrease in dissolved oxygen due to excessive algal growth
Formation of an ozone layer over the river
Increase in pH of the water to neutral
questions.e: Excess fertilizer running into water causes eutrophication; algae grow rapidly, and when they die and decompose, bacteria use up the dissolved oxygen, killing fish and other aquatic organisms.
questions.p: When plenty fertilizer enter river, algae go grow well-well (eutrophication), and when dem die, bacteria go use up the oxygen for water, wey go kill fish and other aquatic animals.

questions.q: A student bubbles a colourless gas through freshly prepared lime water (calcium hydroxide solution) in a test tube. The lime water turns milky (cloudy white). Which gas was most likely passed through the lime water?
questions.e: Carbon(IV) oxide (CO₂) reacts with lime water to form a white insoluble precipitate of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), CaCO₃, which makes the solution milky. This is the standard confirmatory test for CO₂ gas.
questions.p: CO₂ gas dey turn lime water milky because e dey form white CaCO₃ precipitate wey no dey dissolve. Na the standard test wey dem dey use check CO₂ for lab.

questions.q: A gas with a choking smell is produced when ammonium chloride is heated with sodium hydroxide solution. When a piece of moist red litmus paper is held near the mouth of the test tube, the paper turns blue. Which gas is being tested for?
questions.e: Ammonia gas (NH₃) is alkaline and has a sharp, choking smell; it turns moist red litmus paper blue. This is the classic test used to confirm the presence of ammonium ions in a compound.
questions.p: Ammonia gas get strong choking smell and e be alkaline, so e dey turn wet red litmus paper to blue. Na so dem dey test for ammonium ion for compound.

questions.q: Chidinma was given two separate solutions labelled X and Y. Solution X contains iron(II) sulphate while solution Y contains iron(III) chloride, but the labels have fallen off. She adds sodium hydroxide solution dropwise to each. Which observation would correctly help her identify solution Y?
o: A white precipitate forms, which dissolves in excess NaOH
A reddish-brown precipitate forms, insoluble in excess NaOH
A dirty green precipitate forms, insoluble in excess NaOH
questions.e: Iron(III) ions (Fe₃+) react with sodium hydroxide to give a reddish-brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃, which does not dissolve in excess NaOH. Iron(II) ions instead give a dirty green precipitate of Fe(OH)₂, so the reddish-brown colour identifies solution Y as iron(III) chloride.
questions.p: Fe₃+ ion dey react with NaOH give reddish-brown precipitate (Fe(OH)₃) wey no dey dissolve for excess NaOH. Fe₂+ go give dirty green precipitate instead, so reddish-brown na im go show say na Fe₃+ dey solution Y.

questions.q: A colourless salt solution is suspected to contain chloride ions. Dilute trioxonitrate(V) acid (dilute nitric acid) is added, followed by silver trioxonitrate(V) solution. A white precipitate forms. To confirm that the precipitate is indeed silver chloride and not another silver salt, what should be done next?
o: Add excess dilute hydrochloric acid and observe if the precipitate increases
Add excess sodium chloride solution and observe the colour change
Heat the precipitate strongly until it melts
Add dilute (aqueous) ammonia solution and observe if the precipitate dissolves
questions.e: Silver chloride is a white precipitate that readily dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia solution to form a soluble complex, [Ag(NH₃)₂]+. This solubility in dilute ammonia distinguishes it from silver carbonate or silver sulphate precipitates, confirming the presence of chloride ions.
questions.p: Silver chloride na white precipitate wey dey dissolve for dilute ammonia solution because e dey form soluble complex. Dis solubility test dey confirm say na chloride ion dey inside, e dey different from other silver salts.

questions.q: Two white solid salts, P and Q, are each suspected to be either sodium trioxosulphate(IV) (sodium sulphite) or sodium tetraoxosulphate(VI) (sodium sulphate). Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to each solid separately. Salt P produces a colourless gas with a sharp, choking smell that turns acidified potassium heptaoxomanganate(VII) (potassium permanganate) solution from purple to colourless. Salt Q shows no visible reaction. What can be correctly concluded?
o: P is sodium sulphate and Q is sodium sulphite
P is sodium sulphite and Q is sodium sulphate
Both P and Q are sodium sulphate
Both P and Q are sodium sulphite
questions.e: Sulphite ions (SO₃²⁻) react with dilute HCl to release sulphur(IV) oxide gas (SO₂), which has a choking smell and decolourises acidified potassium permanganate due to its reducing property. Sulphate ions (SO₄²⁻) do not react with dilute HCl because they are already fully oxidised, so Q showing no reaction must be sodium sulphate.
questions.p: Sulphite ion (SO₃²⁻) dey react with dilute HCl produce SO₂ gas wey get choking smell and e dey decolourise potassium permanganate because e be reducing agent. Sulphate ion no dey react with dilute HCl at all, so Q wey no show reaction na sodium sulphate.

questions.q: Two colourless salt solutions, R and S, are each known to contain either zinc(II) ions or lead(II) ions. When potassium iodide solution is added dropwise to each, solution R produces a bright yellow precipitate while solution S shows no visible precipitate. Based on this observation, which statement is correct?
o: R contains Zn₂+ and S contains Pb₂+
R contains Pb₂+ and S contains Zn₂+
Both R and S contain Pb₂+
Both R and S contain Zn₂+
questions.e: Lead(II) ions react with potassium iodide to form a characteristic bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide, PbI₂. Zinc(II) ions do not form a precipitate with potassium iodide since zinc iodide is soluble, so solution S with no precipitate must contain Zn₂+.
questions.p: Lead(II) ion dey react with potassium iodide give bright yellow precipitate (PbI₂). Zinc ion no dey form any precipitate with potassium iodide because zinc iodide dey soluble, so S wey no get precipitate na Zn₂+ dey inside.

questions.q: In an acid-base titration, 20.0 cm3 of a sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution of unknown concentration was titrated against 0.10 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid (HCl). The reaction required 24.0 cm3 of the acid for complete neutralization. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH solution.
questions.e: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H₂O, a 1:1 mole ratio. Moles of HCl = 0.024 dm3 x 0.10 mol/dm3 = 0.0024 mol, so moles of NaOH = 0.0024 mol. Concentration of NaOH = 0.0024 mol / 0.020 dm3 = 0.12 mol/dm3.
questions.p: HCl and NaOH dey react 1:1. Moles of HCl = 0.024 x 0.10 = 0.0024 mol, so NaOH moles too na 0.0024 mol. Divide am by 0.020 dm3 give 0.12 mol/dm3.

questions.q: A student titrated 0.1 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid (a strong acid) against 0.1 mol/dm3 ammonia solution (a weak base). The equivalence point of this titration occurs on the acidic side of pH 7, because the salt formed (ammonium chloride) hydrolyses to give an acidic solution. Which indicator is most suitable for detecting the end point of this titration?
questions.e: Methyl orange changes colour within the acidic pH range (about 3.1 to 4.4), which matches where the equivalence point of a strong acid-weak base titration occurs. Phenolphthalein changes colour in the alkaline range, so it is not suitable here.
questions.p: Methyl orange dey change colour for acidic pH range (3.1 to 4.4), and dat na where strong acid-weak base titration equivalence point dey. Phenolphthalein dey change for alkaline side, so e no fit work well here.

questions.q: 25 cm3 of a solution containing 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide per dm3 was titrated against 0.2 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid. Calculate the volume of the acid required for complete neutralization. (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.e: Molar mass of NaOH = 40 g/mol, so concentration of NaOH = 4.0/40 = 0.1 mol/dm3. Moles of NaOH in 25 cm3 = 0.1 x 0.025 = 0.0025 mol, equal to moles of HCl needed (1:1 ratio). Volume of HCl = 0.0025 mol / 0.2 mol/dm3 = 0.0125 dm3 = 12.5 cm3.
questions.p: NaOH molar mass na 40, so concentration = 4.0/40 = 0.1 mol/dm3. Moles for 25cm3 = 0.1 x 0.025 = 0.0025 mol, na im HCl moles too (1:1). Volume = 0.0025/0.2 = 0.0125 dm3 wey be 12.5 cm3.

questions.q: 20 cm3 of 0.05 mol/dm3 sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) was used to completely neutralize 25 cm3 of a sodium hydroxide solution. Given the equation H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH -> Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, calculate the concentration of the NaOH solution.
questions.e: Moles of H₂SO₄ = 0.020 dm3 x 0.05 mol/dm3 = 0.0010 mol. Since the ratio of NaOH to H₂SO₄ is 2:1, moles of NaOH = 2 x 0.0010 = 0.0020 mol. Concentration of NaOH = 0.0020 mol / 0.025 dm3 = 0.08 mol/dm3.
questions.p: H₂SO₄ moles = 0.020 x 0.05 = 0.0010 mol. Since NaOH to H₂SO₄ ratio na 2:1, NaOH moles = 2 x 0.0010 = 0.0020 mol. Concentration = 0.0020/0.025 = 0.08 mol/dm3.

questions.q: 25 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 sodium trioxocarbonate(IV), Na₂CO₃, solution was titrated with 0.2 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid, according to the equation Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the volume of HCl required for complete reaction.
questions.e: Moles of Na₂CO₃ = 0.025 dm3 x 0.1 mol/dm3 = 0.0025 mol. From the equation, moles of HCl needed = 2 x 0.0025 = 0.0050 mol. Volume of HCl = 0.0050 mol / 0.2 mol/dm3 = 0.025 dm3 = 25.0 cm3.
questions.p: Na₂CO₃ moles = 0.025 x 0.1 = 0.0025 mol. From the equation, HCl wey dem need = 2 x 0.0025 = 0.0050 mol. Volume = 0.0050/0.2 = 0.025 dm3 wey be 25.0 cm3.

questions.q: A student dissolved 2.0 g of an impure sample of sodium hydroxide in distilled water and made the solution up to 250 cm3 in a volumetric flask. 25 cm3 of this solution required 20 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid for complete neutralization. Calculate the percentage purity of the NaOH sample. (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.e: Moles of HCl used = 0.020 x 0.15 = 0.0030 mol, which equals moles of NaOH in the 25 cm3 sample (1:1 ratio). Scaling up to 250 cm3 (x10), total moles of pure NaOH = 0.030 mol, giving a mass of 0.030 x 40 = 1.2 g. Percentage purity = (1.2/2.0) x 100 = 60%.
questions.p: HCl wey react = 0.020 x 0.15 = 0.0030 mol, na im NaOH moles too dey for the 25cm3 (1:1). If we scale am go 250cm3 (x10), total pure NaOH moles = 0.030 mol, mass = 0.030 x 40 = 1.2 g. Percentage purity = (1.2/2.0) x 100 = 60%.
